([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

ICRC reporting indicates continued emergency assistance rather than a normalized recovery environment. The ICRC’s Iran operation said it delivered more than 18 metric tons of humanitarian supplies to the Iranian Red Crescent Society on June 15, underscoring persistent medical and civil-defense needs months into the war. IFRC and Red Crescent reporting from earlier in the conflict also documented repeated losses among Iranian Red Crescent responders, highlighting the burden on local relief networks. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/?utm_source=openai))

For the past 24 hours specifically, there are no confirmed comprehensive casualty totals from UN agencies or the ICRC. Reports of drone attacks in Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Iraq show that civilians across the wider region remain exposed to spillover risk even when the U.S.-Iran exchange is paused. The humanitarian implication of the current lull is therefore limited but real: fewer large-scale strikes should reduce immediate civilian harm, yet displacement, infrastructure damage, medical supply gaps and cross-border uncertainty remain entrenched. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/d57e675a7be6dbdd34561909ced240d0?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The key indicators for July 29 will be whether the U.S. strike pause survives another 24 hours, whether Iranian-backed militias continue drone harassment against Gulf states, and whether Oman can translate maritime technical talks into a broader political framework. Markets will watch Hormuz vessel counts at least as closely as headlines from Washington and Tehran, because the real test of de-escalation is not rhetoric but whether commercial shipping starts moving normally again. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/d57e675a7be6dbdd34561909ced240d0?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 149 Intelligence Briefing — July 27, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
A fragile operational pause, rather than a decisive battlefield shift, was the main development over the past 24 hours in the U.S.-Iran theater on Sunday, July 26 into Monday, July 27, 2026. Washington and Tehran both signaled a second consecutive day without major new strikes, easing immediate pressure on oil and equities, but the military situation around the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent Red Sea remains highly unstable. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/ad9fa27d5b1b5fd51e30d923ee738238?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

The most important military fact in the last 24 hours is what did not happen: no confirmed new large-scale U.S. or Iranian strike package was publicly reported during the reporting window, marking a second straight day of paused attacks after roughly two weeks of near-nightly U.S. strikes tied to Iranian threats against shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters, AP, and other outlets reporting on Sunday said President Donald Trump had called off ongoing strikes to give diplomacy “some space,” while an Iranian official said Tehran would also hold fire so long as the U.S. pause remained in place. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/iran-will-halt-attacks-as-long-as-us-maintains-pause-iranian-source-says-after-trump-calls-off-strikes-4552772?utm_source=openai))

That pause follows a period in which U.S. forces had focused on southern Iranian coastal defenses and maritime attack infrastructure intended to degrade Tehran’s ability to menace commercial shipping. Reporting over the past several days indicates the campaign had targeted launch sites, command-and-control positions, and facilities linked to missile, drone, and small-boat operations in the Hormuz battlespace; U.S. officials also suggested preselected target sets were becoming exhausted. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/d491158a4c9a1d3429a87a6ed58f2f72?utm_source=openai))

On the Iranian side, there were likewise no confirmed new missile or drone salvos in the last 24 hours against Gulf states hosting U.S. forces. Tehran’s recent pattern, according to Reuters, had been “attack for attack,” including retaliatory strikes after each night of U.S. bombing; that pattern appears temporarily suspended. There were also no fresh confirmed reports in the last 24 hours of tanker strikes in Hormuz, though the maritime threat environment remains severe after attacks earlier this week and Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping in the Red Sea. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/iran-will-halt-attacks-as-long-as-us-maintains-pause-iranian-source-says-after-trump-calls-off-strikes-4552772?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s line is that the pause is tactical and conditional, not a termination of coercive pressure. U.S.-linked reporting says Trump halted strikes after advice from CENTCOM and other advisers, with the stated objective of creating space for talks rather than conceding freedom of action. U.S. officials have framed the preceding two-week bombing campaign as retaliation for Iranian attacks on shipping and as an effort to degrade Iran’s military capacity along the southern coast and around Hormuz. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/26/hormuz-bombing-pause-trump-iran?utm_source=openai))

Iranian officials and state-aligned messaging are presenting a different narrative: that Tehran’s retaliatory posture forced the U.S. into a pause and that Iran remains committed to reciprocal action, not de-escalation on U.S. terms. Reuters quoted a senior Iranian official as saying Tehran’s position remains “attack for attack,” while AP reported Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei saying talks had made progress and continued. The implication in Iranian messaging is that the U.S. pause reflects battlefield and political limits rather than goodwill. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/iran-will-halt-attacks-as-long-as-us-maintains-pause-iranian-source-says-after-trump-calls-off-strikes-4552772?utm_source=openai))

Israeli messaging remains harder-edged. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on July 26 that he and Trump share a firm position that Iran will not be allowed to rebuild its ballistic missile industry or revive its nuclear program. At the same time, multiple reports note Israel has been notably absent from the most recent U.S. anti-shipping escalation, suggesting either operational compartmentalization or a deliberate effort by Washington to narrow the front. ([main.knesset.gov.il](https://main.knesset.gov.il/en/news/pressreleases/pages/press5126q.aspx?utm_source=openai))

The contradictions are clear. The U.S. casts the pause as diplomacy backed by force; Iran casts it as proof deterrence worked; Israel emphasizes that any pause must not enable Iranian reconstitution. All three narratives contain an element of strategic signaling, and none should be taken at face value without corroboration. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/iran-will-halt-attacks-as-long-as-us-maintains-pause-iranian-source-says-after-trump-calls-off-strikes-4552772?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Markets reacted first and most visibly through oil. Brent crude for October delivery fell 4.6% to $87.48 a barrel, while benchmark U.S. crude for September delivery fell 5.6% to $84.34 after the U.S.-Iran pause held into a second day. Reuters reporting from Singapore similarly said oil prices extended losses by more than 5% on Monday on hopes that a diplomatic track could de-escalate the conflict. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/2fdef9c0b59d90367206d103f0939d30?utm_source=openai))

That drop partly unwinds a sharp risk premium built earlier in the week, when Brent briefly topped $100 a barrel after attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and persistent disruption around Hormuz. The market signal is not that supply risk has disappeared, but that traders now assign a lower probability to immediate all-out escalation in the Gulf over the next several sessions. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45b9165d6c518f5bea668b6ba7a89838?utm_source=openai))

Broader market reaction appears consistent with that interpretation: relief on energy-sensitive assets, but continued volatility where shipping, insurance, and aviation exposure remain high. Reuters earlier this month reported Wall Street weakness alongside renewed strikes, and the recent oil fallback should reduce near-term inflation fears, though only temporarily. The structural issue remains that before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil moved through Hormuz, and traffic there has been repeatedly disrupted. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/oil-jumps-and-bonds-dip-as-us-strikes-iran-4780549?utm_source=openai))

The most important economic takeaway is that prices are now headline-driven. A second day of calm pulled Brent back into the high-$80s, but insurance rates, freight costs, and tanker routing still reflect a conflict zone rather than a normalized market. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/shipping/072226-middle-east-shipping-insurance-costs-rise-on-hormuz-risks-marsh?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a new wave of retail fuel hoarding in Asia, but the region remains exposed to renewed panic buying if either Hormuz or Bab al-Mandeb disruptions intensify. AP reported earlier this week that Southeast Asia remains heavily reliant on Middle Eastern oil and gas and had already been hit hard by supply and price shocks from the Iran war. In the Philippines, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. declared a national energy emergency in March to deter hoarding and profiteering. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/788ceac7b1a80b74881bd5c69e334558?utm_source=openai))

The more immediate story is commercial shipping friction. The Strait of Hormuz remains the central chokepoint, with prior Reuters reporting showing tanker traffic had fallen to a two-month low during renewed strikes. Insurance premiums for Hormuz transits have surged dramatically, with S&P Global reporting rates of 7.5%-10% of hull value as attacks intensified; freight costs for Gulf-to-Asia crude routes also remain elevated. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/hormuz-traffic-slows-to-twomonth-low-as-renewed-us-iran-strikes-raise-safety-risk-4788710?utm_source=openai))

A second supply-chain pressure point is the Red Sea. Iran-aligned Houthis have threatened or attacked Saudi-linked shipping, creating the risk that the conflict could degrade the usefulness of Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline workaround to Yanbu. AP reported Saudi Arabia had recently been exporting around 4 million barrels per day through Yanbu, partially offsetting Hormuz disruption. If Red Sea insecurity persists, that buffer weakens. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/6ee98d611669dc84953d2f2e15958bf9?utm_source=openai))

For Asia-Pacific consumers, the implication is unchanged despite today’s lower oil price: physical supply remains vulnerable, transport costs are still distorted, and another single tanker incident could quickly trigger queues, rationing measures, or precautionary stockpiling. ([spglobal.com](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/shipping/072226-middle-east-shipping-insurance-costs-rise-on-hormuz-risks-marsh?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy gained modest momentum over the last 24 hours, but only in the sense that the guns stayed mostly quiet. AP and Reuters both reported that talks were continuing and that the mutual pause in attacks was being treated by mediators as a positive signal. Iranian spokesman Baghaei said negotiations had made progress, while U.S.-side reporting described Trump as giving talks “some space.” ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/ad9fa27d5b1b5fd51e30d923ee738238?utm_source=openai))

The active mediation architecture still appears to run through regional intermediaries rather than direct U.S.-Iran engagement. Previous Reuters and Axios reporting points to Oman, Qatar, and at times Pakistan as channels for ceasefire and Hormuz-management discussions. A key U.S. objective in earlier talks was an Iranian commitment to keep the Strait of Hormuz open; Tehran, for its part, has sought linkage to broader military and political conditions. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/21/iran-war-ceasefire-proposal-trump-troops?utm_source=openai))

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a formal ceasefire announcement, signed framework, or U.N. Security Council breakthrough. Likewise, no major new public move by China or Russia was confirmed in the reporting window. The diplomatic picture is therefore best understood as a deconfliction pause supported by mediators, not a settlement process with enforceable terms. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/ad9fa27d5b1b5fd51e30d923ee738238?utm_source=openai))

Regional states have the strongest immediate incentive to sustain the pause. Gulf governments remain vulnerable both to Iranian retaliation against bases hosting U.S. forces and to maritime disruption that undermines their export revenues. That shared interest is likely what keeps the mediation track alive despite minimal trust between Washington and Tehran. This is an analytical inference based on the pattern of mediator activity and the economic centrality of Hormuz. ([sahmcapital.com](https://www.sahmcapital.com/news/content/update-2-qatar-pm-in-oman-to-pave-way-for-iran-gulf-iraq-hormuz-talks-2026-06-24?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No authoritative U.N. or ICRC bulletin in the last 24 hours provided a newly updated conflict-wide casualty or displacement total for Iran itself, so the humanitarian picture remains best described as severe but incompletely updated. The latest readily accessible UNHCR regional tracking still shows large-scale displacement effects from the war, including millions temporarily displaced inside Iran earlier in the conflict and significant cross-border movement through Armenia as of mid-July. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

Reuters reported last week that the U.N. human rights chief warned the return to U.S.-Iran hostilities was a major setback for civilians and risked serious disruption to food, medicine, and essential commodities flows. That warning remains relevant even during today’s pause because infrastructure damage and supply bottlenecks do not reverse quickly when air operations stop for 48 hours. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/world-news/return-to-usiran-hostilities-is-huge-setback-for-civilians-un-rights-chief-says-4791331?utm_source=openai))

Available humanitarian reporting continues to emphasize damage to essential systems rather than only battlefield casualties. The ICRC warned that energy, water, and health-care infrastructure had been damaged or destroyed and that hostilities were eroding the foundations of civilian life. Those effects likely persist in coastal provinces and urban areas previously targeted during the maritime-security campaign, though no confirmed 24-hour assessment of fresh damage was available. ([ir.icrc.org](https://ir.icrc.org/en/2026/03/middle-east-hostilities-are-eroding-the-foundations-of-civilian-life/?utm_source=openai))

In practical terms, the humanitarian situation remains characterized by interrupted services, constrained aid access, economic dislocation, and continued civilian vulnerability to a renewed air campaign. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a major new aid corridor, large evacuation, or humanitarian breakthrough. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The key indicator for July 28 will be whether the current mutual pause survives a third day and translates into a structured mediator-led contact, most likely via Oman or Qatar. Markets will watch for any renewed strike activity near Hormuz or fresh tanker incidents, because even a single maritime attack could rapidly reverse today’s de-escalatory momentum in both military and economic terms.

briefingArchive.title: Day 148 Intelligence Briefing — July 26, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The most significant development in the past 24 hours appears to be an operational pause in new U.S. strikes on Iran even as maritime and proxy fronts remained active, with Washington enforcing its blockade and regional spillover continuing through the Red Sea. Markets have reacted by easing slightly from the week’s panic highs, but shipping disruption, stranded crews and continuing rhetoric on civilian infrastructure keep escalation risk elevated. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/25/trump-iran-war-military-directive-strikes?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the clearest confirmed military development was not a major new bombing run but a pause: Axios reported that President Donald Trump directed the U.S. military not to conduct new strikes in Iran on Friday, interrupting what had been nearly two weeks of daily U.S. attacks. That is analytically important because it suggests either a reassessment of escalation risk, an attempt to create diplomatic space, or concern about Iranian retaliation against regional assets and Israel. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/25/trump-iran-war-military-directive-strikes?utm_source=openai))

At sea, however, operations remained kinetic. AP reported Friday that the U.S. military said it fired on another merchant vessel attempting to breach the American blockade of Iranian ports. AP did not identify the ship by name in the excerpt available, but the incident underscores that the naval contest has shifted from blue-water fleet engagements to coercive interdiction, blockade enforcement, and risk management around commercial traffic. The International Maritime Organization said at least 6,000 mariners were stranded on roughly 400 vessels around the Strait of Hormuz, indicating that the battlespace remains heavily militarized despite the U.S. strike pause. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/78c2dbf538f6e61ab816479a4d9bdd85?utm_source=openai))

On the wider regional front, Yemen’s Houthi movement announced missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including facilities in Yanbu and Jizan linked to Aramco, in response to Saudi strikes on Hodeida. This does not prove direct Iranian command and control, but it reinforces the pattern of Tehran-aligned pressure on alternate energy corridors outside Hormuz. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours establish new U.S. or Israeli deep-strike target sets inside Iran, specific munitions used, or verified battle damage assessments beyond the maritime enforcement action and the reported strike pause. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/df3790320c595f3e599fb1dd69423e77?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

U.S. and coalition reporting in the last 24 hours has emphasized maritime control, defensive legitimacy and calibrated use of force. AP, citing the U.S. military, reported that American forces fired on a merchant vessel trying to violate the blockade of Iranian ports. Separately, the earlier operational pattern cited by CBS and AP shows Washington framing its campaign as necessary to preserve or restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, even as actual merchant traffic remains far below normal levels. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/78c2dbf538f6e61ab816479a4d9bdd85?utm_source=openai))

Iranian and pro-Iranian media messaging continues to portray the United States as the escalatory actor and to cast Iranian actions as defensive responses to “aggression.” Press TV material from recent days warned of an “irreparable defeat” for the U.S. if interference in Hormuz continued and said Iran had suspended commercial transit through the strait following renewed American aggression. That framing is propagandistic but consistent: Tehran wants to normalize the idea that it has sovereign veto power over transit conditions in wartime. ([presstv.co.uk](https://www.presstv.co.uk/Detail/2026/07/23/772822/Iran-IRGC-warning-United-States-Strait-of-Hormuz?utm_source=openai))

Israel’s public posture appears more anticipatory than declaratory in the past 24 hours. Axios reported that Israeli officials expected another round of U.S. strikes on Friday and prepared for a possible large U.S. attack that could trigger Iranian retaliation against Israel. That suggests Israel remains closely integrated into escalation planning, even if no new Israeli combat communiqué dominated the last day’s reporting. The Times of Israel reported earlier this week that blasts heard near Eilat did not reflect missile impacts inside Israeli territory, illustrating the continuing Israeli effort to reassure the domestic public while remaining on alert. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/25/trump-iran-war-military-directive-strikes?utm_source=openai))

The major contradiction remains over control of Hormuz: Washington says it is open except to Iran-linked shipping, while Iranian messaging implies the waterway’s old status quo is over. In practice, the shipping data supports neither side’s maximalist narrative; the strait is not fully closed, but it is functioning far below normal commercial levels. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/22/trump-iran-bridges-power-plants-hormuz?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Oil remains the central market transmission channel. AP reported Friday that Brent crude fell 3.9% to $96.78 a barrel, the first decline in a week, after having earlier pushed above $100 during the latest Hormuz and Red Sea escalations. Before the war began in late February, Brent had traded around $72. That pullback suggests markets took some comfort from the absence of a fresh U.S. strike wave and from profit-taking after the week’s fear bid, but prices remain at crisis-elevated levels. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0b9c3b2aa5ca83eb391c1388efe03c97?utm_source=openai))

Broader equity markets have remained choppy rather than disorderly. Recent Reuters and AP market reporting showed Wall Street and global risk assets weakening as oil spiked, with the S&P 500 suffering its worst day of July during the sharpest part of the latest escalation cycle. The immediate pattern is classic conflict pricing: energy up, transport and rate-sensitive sectors pressured, while investors reassess inflation and central-bank implications. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/newsletters/axios-closer-12b3590f-4896-42a7-a286-393f932272d5?utm_source=openai))

The bigger macro issue is not just spot crude but disruption to trade flows and insurance. Reuters reporting this week showed vessel crossings in Hormuz dropping sharply, with daily sailings far below the prewar average of roughly 125. That reduction in throughput amplifies freight costs, war-risk premiums and refinery feedstock uncertainty, especially in Asia. Markets are therefore reacting not only to physical damage risk but to the erosion of confidence in maritime reliability. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/hormuz-vessel-crossings-fall-further-as-security-concerns-linger-4804603?utm_source=openai))

No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provided fresh benchmark numbers for WTI, gold or major industrial commodities beyond Brent’s pullback. Still, the war’s economic signal remains clear: even when oil eases on a given day, the structural risk premium tied to Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remains embedded. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0b9c3b2aa5ca83eb391c1388efe03c97?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

Consumer-level disruption is most visible in fuel and shipping stress rather than universal panic buying. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours established new large-scale public fuel hoarding episodes in Asia-Pacific, but the region remains acutely exposed. AP, citing the International Energy Agency, reported earlier this week that Asian markets imported about 80% of the crude oil and almost 90% of the LNG transiting Hormuz in 2025, making Southeast and East Asia particularly vulnerable to prolonged disruption. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/12b3a257be0b6af9d96356dd78be3cfd?utm_source=openai))

On the logistics side, the evidence is stronger. Reuters reported this week that Hormuz vessel crossings fell further, with only isolated cargo movements visible in Kpler data. Earlier Reuters reporting also said some shipowners were refusing U.S.-military-guided transit schemes, showing that convoy-style reassurance has not restored commercial confidence. That means even where passage is technically possible, insurers, operators and charterers may still choose delay or rerouting. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/hormuz-vessel-crossings-fall-further-as-security-concerns-linger-4804603?utm_source=openai))

The IMO’s own figures underline the scale of disruption: more than 20,000 seafarers are affected in the region, and the organization says its primary concern remains the safety of crews on ships operating in and around Hormuz. AP separately reported at least 6,000 mariners stranded on about 400 vessels around the strait. These two figures are not contradictory; they likely reflect different counting methodologies for directly stranded crews versus all affected personnel in the wider operational zone. ([imo.org](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/middle-east-strait-of-hormuz.aspx?utm_source=openai))

In downstream energy markets, Singapore’s role as Asia’s refining and storage hub remains critical. Reuters reported in June that Singapore oil product inventories had slumped to a near 13-year low as Middle East shipments stayed curtailed. That is not a last-24-hour update, but it explains why even modest additional disruption could rapidly feed into regional shortages, queueing, or precautionary stockpiling. ([uk.marketscreener.com](https://uk.marketscreener.com/news/singapore-s-oil-product-inventories-slump-to-near-13-year-low-ce7f5cdbd080f621?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomatically, the key signal is that talks are not dead even though the ceasefire framework is. Reuters reported on July 10 that Trump said Iran had asked to continue talks and that the United States had agreed, while stressing the June ceasefire was over. That remains the best evidence that an off-ramp still exists, albeit one disconnected from a functioning truce on the ground. ([theprint.in](https://theprint.in/world/trump-says-us-agreed-to-irans-request-to-continue-talks-but-ceasefire-is-over/2983381/?utm_source=openai))

Over the last 24 hours, Axios reported that the U.S. and U.K. are planning a high-level meeting in London next week focused on building an international coalition to protect shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. That matters because it suggests Washington is trying to multilateralize what has become an increasingly unilateral and politically costly maritime campaign. It also indicates that maritime security, rather than a broader political settlement, may be the most realistic near-term diplomatic objective. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/07/24/hormuz-us-uk-conference-iran?utm_source=openai))

At the UN level, the latest authoritative public messaging remains older than 24 hours. The Secretary-General urged Iran and the U.S. on July 12 to urgently resume negotiations as renewed strikes raised fears of full-scale war. Earlier UN statements also called for navigational freedoms to be restored in line with international law. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours show a new Security Council breakthrough or formal ceasefire mechanism. ([un.org](https://www.un.org/en/un-chief-urges-iran-and-us-%E2%80%98urgently-resume-negotiations%E2%80%99-gulf-strikes-escalate?utm_source=openai))

China and Russia remain important but publicly cautious. Reuters reported on July 24 that Trump warned both countries against involvement and said Putin had told him Russia would not sell weapons to Iran; that is a U.S. claim, not independent confirmation from Moscow. Gulf states continue to balance de-escalation rhetoric with operational hedging, especially as Houthi attacks now threaten Saudi-linked Red Sea routes as well as Hormuz traffic. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-warns-china-russia-against-involvement-in-iran-war-4812264?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

The humanitarian picture remains severe, though hard real-time casualty accounting in the last 24 hours is limited. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provided a fresh comprehensive civilian death toll. The most recent credible humanitarian baselines available from major institutions remain older: UNHCR said in March that up to 3.2 million Iranians were temporarily displaced inside the country, and its July regional data showed 544,300 crossings by Iranians into neighboring countries since February 28, with movements especially fluid through Armenia and Türkiye. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

Recent reporting indicates infrastructure impacts are worsening civilian risk. AP said yesterday that recent U.S. strikes disrupted transportation and communications within Iran and damaged water infrastructure used by thousands of people. Earlier AP reporting this week also said two people were killed in a U.S. missile strike in Shalamcheh, according to Iranian state media. Those claims require caution because battlefield casualty narratives are politicized, but they fit the wider trend of strikes increasingly affecting dual-use and civilian-reliant systems. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/d7744d3063116944d49a616c007d669c?utm_source=openai))

The ICRC warned in April that any return to large-scale war would be catastrophic for millions of civilians in Iran and across the region. That warning now looks prescient rather than hypothetical. In addition to Iranian civilians, UNHCR notes that around 1.65 million forcibly displaced people of different documentation statuses reside in Iran, including large numbers of Afghan refugees, making secondary humanitarian spillover a major concern. ([icrc.org](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/iran-icrc-president-says-return-war-would-be-ruinous-civilians?utm_source=openai))

At sea, humanitarian issues overlap with supply-chain stress. The IMO says more than 20,000 seafarers are affected in the region, with thousands previously evacuated and many others still exposed to attack, detention or prolonged stranding. That makes the maritime dimension not only an economic crisis but a human one. ([imo.org](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/middle-east-strait-of-hormuz.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: The main indicators to watch tomorrow are whether the reported U.S. pause in strikes holds, whether Iran or allied groups test that pause through Hormuz or Red Sea attacks, and whether tanker traffic shows any measurable rebound. Markets will be highly sensitive to any fresh bridge, power-grid or port strikes inside Iran, because that would signal a shift from coercive maritime warfare toward broader infrastructure escalation.

briefingArchive.title: Day 147 Intelligence Briefing — July 25, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The past 24 hours were defined by continued U.S. strikes on Iranian military infrastructure tied to the Strait of Hormuz crisis, coupled with fresh Iranian attacks on U.S.-linked positions in the Gulf and new maritime security alarms. The most consequential development is that the military contest is increasingly centered on shipping protection and blockade enforcement rather than a single decisive land campaign, even as oil remains near triple digits and diplomacy continues in parallel. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4554310/us-concludes-13th-night-of-strikes-on-iranian-military-targets/))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, U.S. and coalition military activity remained focused on degrading Iranian capabilities used to threaten commercial shipping and coalition positions. CENTCOM said it completed a 13th consecutive night of strikes on July 23 at 9 p.m. ET, targeting Iranian command centers, drone storage facilities, communications networks, coastal surveillance sites, and maritime capabilities. A separate July 22 release said U.S. forces also struck missile and drone storage facilities and air defense assets, while continuing a maritime blockade posture; CENTCOM stated it has redirected nine commercial vessels and disabled one to enforce the blockade of Iranian ports. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4554310/us-concludes-13th-night-of-strikes-on-iranian-military-targets/))

Open-source reporting indicates the geographic scope of strikes widened further. AP reported blasts on Qeshm Island, a site associated with Iranian naval and drone-boat activity in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as strikes in Isfahan province, home to a major Iranian air base and one of Iran’s nuclear sites. AP also reported that, according to Iranian semi-official media, a Revolutionary Guard naval base in northern Iran was struck. These reports are consistent with a U.S. strategy of targeting both the southern coastal threat architecture and deeper support nodes. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/78c2dbf538f6e61ab816479a4d9bdd85?utm_source=openai))

Iran responded through dispersed regional retaliation rather than a single massed salvo. Reuters reported Iranian fire at U.S. bases in neighboring Arab states after the latest U.S. strikes, while Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday. Saudi-linked reporting also tied the wider escalation to Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, suggesting Tehran and its partners are now contesting both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-missiles-hit-iran-as-trump-still-holds-out-for-a-deal-4752853?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S. narrative, led by CENTCOM and reinforced by White House messaging, emphasizes defensive necessity and maritime security. CENTCOM says its strikes are precision attacks intended to reduce Iran’s ability to threaten civilian mariners and commercial vessels, and insists the Strait of Hormuz remains open with U.S. military support. U.S. officials also frame the campaign as a measured response to Iranian attacks on shipping and regional bases rather than a return to the maximal early-war air campaign. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4554310/us-concludes-13th-night-of-strikes-on-iranian-military-targets/))

Iranian state and state-aligned media are presenting a very different picture. Iranian military statements carried by state television said U.S. targets in Bahrain, Jordan, and Kuwait were struck in retaliation, with specific claims that Arash kamikaze drones hit fuel tanks, warehouses, silos, and barracks at Isa Air Base in Bahrain. Reuters, citing Iranian and U.S. accounts, reported an IRGC claim that it hit a U.S. electronic warfare unit at Al-Adiri base in Kuwait and caused unspecified casualties. Press TV coverage in recent days has similarly highlighted “successful” retaliatory strikes on U.S. regional infrastructure. ([euronews.com](https://www.euronews.com/2026/07/24/iran-military-says-it-targeted-us-bases-in-bahrain-jordan-and-kuwait?utm_source=openai))

Israel’s reporting in the past 24 hours has been less central than during earlier phases of the war, but Israeli-aligned and international coverage continues to portray the current round as part of a broader effort to compel Tehran back into a restrictive deal while containing escalation at sea. The propaganda gap remains wide: Washington stresses restored freedom of navigation, while independent maritime reporting and AP coverage show continued vessel attacks, rerouting, and large numbers of stranded mariners. Iranian media, for its part, inflate tactical success and casualties but provide little independently verifiable battle damage evidence. The most reliable analytic judgment is that both sides are selectively truthful: the U.S. is degrading Iranian systems, but not yet restoring normal maritime conditions; Iran is retaining enough capability to sustain disruption and retaliatory signaling. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4554310/us-concludes-13th-night-of-strikes-on-iranian-military-targets/))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy markets remain the clearest real-time barometer of escalation risk. Brent crude fell 3.9% on July 24 to $96.78 a barrel after previously topping $100 earlier in the week, according to AP market coverage. Reuters reported Brent settled at $94.07 on July 22, up 3.36% on the day and its highest level since June 11, after touching $95.47 intraday. Taken together, the price action suggests a persistent conflict premium remains embedded even when markets temporarily retrace on profit-taking or hopes of diplomacy. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0b9c3b2aa5ca83eb391c1388efe03c97?utm_source=openai))

Equities have reacted unevenly rather than in full panic. AP reported the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 235.60 points, or 0.5%, at 51,947.25 on July 24 even as all major indexes lost ground for the week under pressure from the war. Earlier in the week, the S&P 500 fell 10.24 points to 7,498.96 and the Nasdaq dropped 146.30 points to 25,690.90 as oil climbed and investors weighed inflation and earnings risks. Reuters and market coverage have repeatedly linked higher energy prices to renewed concern over inflation, transport costs, and central-bank tightening risk. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/0b9c3b2aa5ca83eb391c1388efe03c97?utm_source=openai))

The broader economic signal is not just the absolute oil price but the threat to transit routes. Reuters reported widening backwardation in Brent futures, a sign of tight near-term supply, while AP noted Brent was trading near $72 before the current July re-escalation. That delta underscores that the market is pricing not merely war headlines, but concrete risk to seaborne flows and refining chains. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/oil-prices-rise-slightly-after-us-announces-new-round-of-strikes-on-iran-4804503?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The consumer and logistics picture is worsening most visibly around maritime chokepoints and Asian fuel dependence. AP reported that Saudi Arabia has been forced to divert millions of barrels a day to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, a sign that the disruption is no longer hypothetical. At the same time, the International Maritime Organization said at least 6,000 mariners are stranded on about 400 vessels around the Strait, while the IMO’s own July 8 statement said hundreds of ships and nearly 6,000 seafarers remained trapped in the Gulf amid attacks and evacuation pauses. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/78c2dbf538f6e61ab816479a4d9bdd85?utm_source=openai))

Direct confirmed reporting of fresh retail fuel panic-buying in the last 24 hours is limited. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a new wave of mass consumer hoarding at gas stations across Asia-Pacific. However, the region remains highly vulnerable. Earlier regional reporting documented fuel rationing, LPG hoarding, and jet-fuel stockpiling in parts of Asia during previous spikes, and current conditions point to renewed pressure rather than relief. Reuters and industry reporting have also shown some ships refusing U.S.-guided Hormuz transits because of safety concerns, while four oil and gas tankers turned back earlier in July after vessel attacks. ([straitstimes.com](https://www.straitstimes.com/asia/ill-be-the-one-to-lose-hawkers-drivers-in-asia-brace-themselves-for-fuel-shortage-amid-iran-war?utm_source=openai))

The secondary front in the Red Sea compounds the supply-chain shock. Reuters reported Houthi threats and attacks against Saudi-linked shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb area, and AP reported Saudi strikes on Hodeida in response. The practical effect is that importers and refiners in Asia face simultaneous uncertainty on both the Gulf source side and the outbound shipping side. Even where physical shortages are not yet acute, freight, insurance, and rerouting costs are rising. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/trump-vows-to-punish-iran-and-houthis-for-attacks-in-red-sea-4810448?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy is active but not yet producing de-escalation. Oman remains the most visible intermediary. AP reported an Omani diplomatic delegation was in Tehran on Friday to discuss management of shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, while Axios reported the U.S. and U.K. are preparing a high-level London meeting next week aimed at building an international maritime protection coalition. Axios also reported that previous Oman-Iran-Qatar negotiations on a new Hormuz arrangement ended without results, helping explain the renewed military phase. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/78c2dbf538f6e61ab816479a4d9bdd85?utm_source=openai))

Washington’s messaging remains dual-track: military pressure paired with conditional openness to a deal. Reuters reported President Trump again left open the door to diplomacy even while threatening “major military punishment” for Iran and the Houthis. Straits Times reporting similarly said Trump is weighing a broader offensive as leverage to force a peace arrangement. This is coercive diplomacy rather than conventional ceasefire making. ([ca.investing.com](https://ca.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-missiles-hit-iran-as-trump-still-holds-out-for-a-deal-4752853?utm_source=openai))

Regional and international positioning remains cautious. Straits Times reported Trump publicly warned China and Russia against direct involvement, while Gulf states continue balancing support for U.S. protection with fear of becoming retaliation platforms. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours indicate a formal ceasefire framework, UN-backed truce text, or announced breakthrough in back-channel negotiations. The current diplomatic pattern is crisis management around shipping rather than a credible pathway to a comprehensive end to hostilities. ([straitstimes.com](https://www.straitstimes.com/world/middle-east/trump-warns-china-russia-against-involvement-in-iran-war?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

The humanitarian situation continues to deteriorate, though fresh verified casualty totals from the last 24 hours are scarce. No confirmed reports in the last 24 hours provide a new authoritative UN or ICRC civilian casualty count for Iran or the wider theater. That absence should not be read as stability. The conflict continues to damage infrastructure, displace civilians, and endanger migrant and refugee populations already under severe strain. ([icrc.org](https://www.icrc.org/en/news-release/iran-icrc-president-says-return-war-would-be-ruinous-civilians?utm_source=openai))

The most authoritative displacement baseline remains UNHCR’s March assessment that up to 3.2 million people were temporarily displaced inside Iran, primarily from Tehran and other major urban centers, with later UNHCR regional material warning of rising protection risks for refugees, especially Afghans and Iraqis already in Iran. UNHCR data through early July also indicated continued cross-border movement by Iranian nationals into Armenia, though not yet a mass refugee exodus into Iraq. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

At sea, the humanitarian dimension is immediate and concrete. The IMO says nearly 6,000 seafarers remain stranded and under psychological strain because safe evacuation from the Gulf cannot be assured. This matters analytically because the maritime crisis is not only an economic chokepoint but also a civilian protection issue involving multinational crews trapped in a war zone. Infrastructure targeting has also widened concerns beyond oil: recent reporting has flagged attacks and threats involving desalination and civilian-adjacent facilities in the Gulf, raising the risk of broader public-service disruption if escalation continues. ([imo.org](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/pressbriefings/pages/imo-secretary-general-condemns-new-attacks-on-ships-in-strait-of-hormuz.aspx?utm_source=openai))

## Outlook

The key indicators for July 26 will be whether Iran sustains regional retaliatory strikes at the current tempo, whether U.S. attacks continue to widen beyond southern coastal targets, and whether the Oman-led shipping talks produce any practical deconfliction mechanism. Markets will focus on whether Brent holds below $100 or resumes its climb, while the most important operational signal will be whether commercial shipping volume through or around Hormuz improves materially rather than merely remaining nominally “open.” ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/Article/4554310/us-concludes-13th-night-of-strikes-on-iranian-military-targets/))

briefingArchive.title: Day 146 Intelligence Briefing — July 24, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The past 24 hours were defined by a renewed maritime escalation rather than a decisive shift on land. U.S. forces moved into a 13th consecutive night of strikes tied to the Strait of Hormuz fight, while Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea pushed Brent briefly above $100 a barrel and widened concern that the conflict is now threatening both major regional oil corridors at once. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the clearest confirmed military development was the continuation of U.S. strike operations against Iran linked to maritime security and the campaign to restore commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command said the attacks were intended to “further degrade Iran’s ability to threaten civilian mariners and commercial vessels transiting regional waters,” indicating an operational focus on anti-shipping capabilities, coastal launch infrastructure, and associated command-and-control nodes rather than a major new ground phase. AP reported this marked the 13th night of strikes. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

A separate official U.S. government release published July 23 said American forces this month have hit “dozens of Iranian military sites on land” and resumed a blockade posture at sea. The same release said CENTCOM has redirected nine commercial vessels and disabled one to keep ships from entering or departing Iranian ports, underscoring that the maritime campaign has expanded beyond escort and interception into coercive traffic control. ([war.gov](https://www.war.gov/News/News-Stories/Article/Article/4553395/centcom-completes-latest-strikes-against-iran/))

On the broader theater picture, there were no widely confirmed public details in the last 24 hours on specific aircraft types, munitions loads, or named Iranian inland targets struck overnight. Likewise, there were no independently confirmed reports in the last 24 hours of major Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Israel or U.S. regional bases. The most immediate non-U.S. military action was by Yemen’s Houthis, who claimed strikes on the Saudi tankers Encelia and Layla in the Red Sea, with Saudi and UK maritime reporting confirming at least one tanker fire and projectile impact reporting southwest of Saudi Arabia. The operational significance is substantial: pressure on Hormuz is now being paired with threat pressure on Bab el-Mandeb, complicating coalition maritime rerouting. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

Washington’s public line remains narrow and functional: the Pentagon and CENTCOM are framing current attacks as limited, retaliatory, and protective of freedom of navigation. The key U.S. message is that strikes are aimed at degrading Iran’s capacity to threaten commercial shipping, not at announcing a wholly new war aim. A Defense Department release also emphasized blockade enforcement and vessel diversion, suggesting the administration wants to present the current phase as maritime stabilization even as the scope of action has plainly expanded. ([war.gov](https://www.war.gov/News/News-Stories/Article/Article/4553395/centcom-completes-latest-strikes-against-iran/))

Iranian official and state-aligned messaging, by contrast, continues to frame all U.S. operations as illegal aggression and to present Iranian actions as self-defense against attacks on national territory, shipping, and civilian infrastructure. In the last 24 hours, however, I found no fresh English-language IRNA or Press TV report with independently verifiable new battlefield claims dated July 23-24. The latest accessible Iranian state narratives in search results remain consistent with earlier patterns: alleged U.S. ceasefire violations, claims of successful retaliatory strikes on U.S. naval assets, and portrayal of maritime confrontation as resistance to unlawful Western interference. ([www2.irna.ir](https://www2.irna.ir/en?utm_source=openai))

Israeli official reporting in the last 24 hours appears limited in publicly accessible English releases tied directly to this latest overnight cycle. No confirmed Israeli readout surfaced in the search results detailing fresh long-range strikes or battle damage assessments for July 23-24. That absence itself is notable and may reflect operational silence, a U.S.-led maritime phase, or simply a lag in publication. ([m.www.idf.il](https://m.www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/idf-press-releases-israel-at-war/?page=23&utm_source=openai))

The contradiction set remains familiar: the U.S. side stresses precision and shipping protection; Iranian outlets stress sovereignty, civilian harm, and U.S. escalation; Houthi-aligned messaging seeks to portray Red Sea attacks as an extension of anti-U.S. pressure. None of the sides provide a neutral accounting of damage, and battlefield claims from Tehran and its partners remain especially difficult to verify independently in real time. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

## Market & Economic Impact

Markets reacted first and foremost to shipping risk. Brent crude briefly touched $102 per barrel on July 23 and moved above the $100 threshold, its highest level since May for the front contract, while AP reported Wall Street weakened as investors absorbed both higher oil and major tech-stock declines. The oil move was directly tied to the Houthi attack on Saudi tankers and the renewed sense that neither Hormuz nor Red Sea bypass routes can be assumed secure. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/45b9165d6c518f5bea668b6ba7a89838))

The market logic is straightforward: a conflict that had already disrupted the Strait of Hormuz is now threatening alternative export routes. Before the war, roughly 15 million barrels per day of Persian Gulf oil moved through Hormuz, and AP noted that Saudi Arabia has recently been diverting millions of barrels per day to Yanbu on the Red Sea via overland pipeline. That workaround is now under pressure as well. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/c492604ca2bf139c6d7db7065c951ff1?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets reflected broader risk aversion, though sector performance was mixed. Energy shares outperformed in premarket Reuters reporting as Brent tested $100, while broader U.S. indices came under pressure. Investors are increasingly treating the Iran theater less as a short-lived geopolitical premium and more as a recurring inflationary shock with second-order effects on freight, insurance, and central-bank expectations. ([au.investing.com](https://au.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-energy-shares-gain-as-houthi-tanker-attacks-push-brent-to-100-4549404?utm_source=openai))

The structural concern is that buffers are thinning. The IMF said on July 15 that the oil market had absorbed the war shock but that buffers were running low, with diesel and jet fuel among the most stressed refined-product categories. That matters because even if crude supply rerouting continues, refined-product bottlenecks can still transmit inflation quickly into transport, food, and manufacturing chains. ([imf.org](https://www.imf.org/en/blogs/articles/2026/07/15/the-oil-market-absorbed-the-war-shock-but-buffers-are-running-low?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

There are no confirmed new reports in the last 24 hours of mass panic buying at retail fuel stations across Asia on the scale seen in March, but the supply-chain picture worsened materially. The main reason is that the Red Sea attacks now threaten Saudi exports from Yanbu, one of the principal workarounds used to blunt the impact of Hormuz disruption. Lloyd’s List Intelligence described this as a “double whammy” for oil shipments. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

The Asia-Pacific region remains highly exposed. AP reported Southeast Asia has been hit hard by the war-driven energy shock because of its reliance on Middle Eastern oil and gas, while earlier emergency measures remain in place in some states, including the Philippines’ March energy emergency intended to prevent hoarding and profiteering. That does not prove fresh hoarding in the last 24 hours, but it does show governments remain on a defensive footing because renewed price spikes can quickly revive retail shortages and public anxiety. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/12b3a257be0b6af9d96356dd78be3cfd?utm_source=openai))

Consumer effects are already visible through prices. AP reported higher fuel costs are feeding into truckload pricing, groceries, school supplies, and other shipped goods, with an AFS Logistics/TD Cowen Freight Index released July 14 showing truckload pricing at a four-year high due partly to rising fuel costs and capacity constraints. In practical terms, the war’s maritime disruptions are no longer just an energy story; they are propagating into broad consumer inflation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/5cdf2386055896c1dfc4d9499196b085?utm_source=openai))

Shipping safety remains a major bottleneck. The IMO says around 20,000 seafarers, plus port and offshore workers, are affected in the region. Its Hormuz evacuation framework remains paused, and IMO data show a large pool of ships and crews still under operational strain. Even absent visible fuel queues today, these conditions point to continued volatility in deliveries, bunker availability, insurance rates, and port scheduling across Asia-bound routes. ([imo.org](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/middle-east-strait-of-hormuz.aspx))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active rhetorically but weak operationally. I found no confirmed breakthrough in the last 24 hours on ceasefire restoration or a new U.S.-Iran negotiating channel producing concrete de-escalation terms. The dominant signal instead is that combat actions are again outpacing diplomacy. AP described the strikes earlier this week as overshadowing diplomatic efforts, and the current maritime exchange reinforces that assessment. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

The UN position remains centered on restraint and ceasefire preservation. A UN political affairs statement from July 2 had already urged maximum restraint to preserve the U.S.-Iran ceasefire, while referencing U.S. claims that Iranian actions against commercial shipping had prompted military responses. That framing still maps onto the present moment: the diplomatic architecture exists, but its enforcement credibility has eroded sharply since the July 7 collapse of the previous ceasefire arrangement. ([dppa.un.org](https://dppa.un.org/en/speeches-and-statements/un-calls-for-maximum-restraint-to-preserve-ceasefire-between-the?utm_source=openai))

Regionally, Gulf producers are focusing as much on export continuity as on mediation. The scramble to expand bypass infrastructure around Hormuz shows that Gulf states are preparing for prolonged insecurity, not an imminent settlement. Saudi use of Red Sea routes, and the vulnerability of those routes to Houthi action, will likely intensify quiet Gulf pressure for stronger maritime protection while avoiding open political ownership of escalation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/896c02f0c978986fff0ae7fc389ea51f))

China and Russia were not prominent in the past 24 hours’ top reporting with new mediation proposals. No confirmed fresh public initiative from Beijing or Moscow emerged in the search results today. In intelligence terms, the diplomatic picture is best assessed as stalled: channels likely exist, back-channel contacts almost certainly continue, but there is no evidence from the last 24 hours that they are translating into reduced military tempo. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/be298023201a3e4b709b11372aa6e045?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

No comprehensive new 24-hour casualty tally for civilians in Iran or the wider theater was confirmed in the accessible reporting. That gap is important: battlefield reporting remains dominated by maritime and military updates, while humanitarian accounting is lagging and contested. In such conditions, casualty figures should be treated cautiously unless attributed to named international agencies or multiple independent outlets. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

What is confirmed is that the maritime crisis itself has a humanitarian dimension. The IMO says around 20,000 seafarers and associated maritime workers are affected in the region, and earlier IMO reporting documented at least 46 confirmed attacks on international shipping with 14 seafarer fatalities since February 28. A later incidents page listed 61 confirmed incidents as of July 21, indicating that the burden on civilian crews continues to accumulate even when headline reporting focuses on state militaries. ([imo.org](https://www.imo.org/en/mediacentre/hottopics/pages/middle-east-strait-of-hormuz.aspx))

Inside Iran, the broader civilian displacement baseline remains severe. UNHCR said in March that up to 3.2 million Iranians were temporarily displaced by the conflict. I found no updated UNHCR nationwide displacement number issued in the last 24 hours, so the prudent judgment is that the humanitarian picture remains serious but under-refreshed in public reporting today. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

Infrastructure risks also remain high. AP has reported in recent days that Iran has targeted energy infrastructure and desalination facilities in neighboring Gulf states in response to U.S. attacks, which raises civilian vulnerability far beyond immediate strike zones by threatening water and power access. The humanitarian situation therefore should not be read solely through body counts; it also includes prolonged displacement, shipping insecurity, and the degradation of civilian-essential infrastructure across the Gulf theater. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/60d46bf8c83c43a8f2268b7b87627c55))

Outlook

The key indicator for July 25 will be whether the conflict remains a controlled maritime-air campaign or broadens into a dual-chokepoint crisis spanning both Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. Watch for three things: any CENTCOM battle-damage detail on overnight strikes, any verified Iranian retaliation against regional bases or shipping, and whether oil holds above $100, which would signal markets now expect prolonged disruption rather than a temporary shock.

briefingArchive.title: Day 145 Intelligence Briefing — July 23, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The past 24 hours were defined by continued U.S. air operations against Iranian military infrastructure and a parallel intensification of coercive signaling around civilian and commercial targets. Markets absorbed the renewed escalation with oil pushing back into the low-$90s per barrel range, while diplomacy remained active but visibly lagged the operational tempo. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/42ff3de8d135ad72ff3ba4d94cc0921d?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the main confirmed military development was the continuation of U.S. strikes into Iran for a 12th consecutive night, according to AP reporting and statements attributed to CENTCOM. The U.S. side says the latest wave hit military operations centers, maritime capabilities, aircraft hangars, drone storage facilities, and logistics infrastructure, with the stated objective of further degrading Iran’s ability to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. A prior CENTCOM summary of the campaign says U.S. forces have already conducted hundreds of strikes against Iranian missile, drone, air defense, airfield, and command-and-control targets, indicating this latest round is part of a sustained attritional air campaign rather than a discrete raid. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/42ff3de8d135ad72ff3ba4d94cc0921d?utm_source=openai))

Iranian responses in the last day appear to have centered less on large-volume direct missile salvos and more on continued pressure against regional infrastructure and maritime traffic. AP reported that Iran has targeted energy infrastructure and desalination facilities in neighboring Gulf states, while the broader maritime picture remains unstable after repeated tanker incidents in and around Hormuz earlier this week. The U.S. military has also continued blockade enforcement measures; AP reported earlier that CENTCOM had redirected eight commercial vessels and disabled one non-compliant ship as part of its maritime control effort. No independently verified evidence emerged in the last 24 hours of a major new Iranian naval engagement, but the battlespace remains highly contested. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/42ff3de8d135ad72ff3ba4d94cc0921d?utm_source=openai))

Weapon-system detail remains only partially confirmed in the latest 24-hour reporting. CENTCOM’s campaign imagery and prior releases show use of Tomahawk cruise missiles from surface combatants and a mixed manned-unmanned strike architecture, while the Epic Fury fact sheet lists MQ-9s and other fixed- and rotary-wing assets in theater. No official last-24-hour battle damage assessment beyond claimed target categories has been released. ([centcom.mil](https://www.centcom.mil/MEDIA/PUBLIC-RELEASES/RUSSIAN-PUBLIC-RELEASES/Russian-Press-Release-View/Article/4514383//?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S./coalition narrative remains consistent: Washington is framing operations as precision strikes against military targets linked to Iranian threats to regional security and commercial navigation. CENTCOM-linked reporting says the latest targets were military operations centers, maritime capabilities, hangars, drone storage sites, and logistics nodes, all tied to degrading Iran’s strike capacity around Hormuz. Pentagon-associated messaging in recent weeks has also emphasized that the broader campaign has badly damaged Iranian ballistic missile, drone, air defense, and airfield capacity, projecting an image of steady operational success and diminishing Iranian capability. ([timesofisrael.com](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/centcom-says-latest-us-strikes-on-iran-targeted-military-ops-centers-aircraft-hangers-and-drone-storage-sites/?utm_source=openai))

Iranian state reporting, by contrast, has emphasized nationwide explosions across multiple provinces and portrayed U.S. and Israeli attacks as unlawful aggression that increasingly strikes civilian-adjacent infrastructure. AP, citing IRNA, reported explosions in several provinces in recent days; Iranian officials in UN fora have accused Washington of attacking civilian infrastructure and violating prior understandings. Tehran’s external messaging also continues to argue that pressure on Gulf shipping is a consequence of war and blockade rather than unprovoked escalation. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

Israel’s public line has been less central in the last 24 hours than CENTCOM’s, but Israeli reporting has amplified U.S. operational claims, including the description of strikes on hangars, drone storage, and maritime-related facilities. The key contradiction remains over target character: Washington presents the campaign as focused on military enablers, while Iran stresses civilian harm and infrastructure effects. That gap is widened by the information environment itself: all sides are using selective disclosure, and independent verification inside Iran remains limited. A prudent analytic judgment is that both narratives contain elements of truth, but each is structured for domestic and international influence operations as much as for factual reporting. ([timesofisrael.com](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/centcom-says-latest-us-strikes-on-iran-targeted-military-ops-centers-aircraft-hangers-and-drone-storage-sites/?utm_source=openai))

## Market & Economic Impact

Energy markets reacted immediately to the renewed strikes and continuing shipping risk. Reuters market coverage carried by MarketScreener said oil rose to a six-week high on July 23 as U.S. and Iranian strikes continued, with Brent climbing above $93 a barrel in broader reporting from AP. Earlier this week AP had put Brent above $88, and over the weekend above $90, underscoring a sharp re-risking of crude as traders concluded that the collapse of the interim ceasefire had restored a serious Hormuz disruption premium. ([au.marketscreener.com](https://au.marketscreener.com/news/oil-prices-jump-on-us-iran-strikes-stocks-flat-ahead-of-big-tech-results-ce7f51d9dc8ff72c?utm_source=openai))

Equity markets have so far treated the conflict as a serious but not yet systemic shock. Reuters reporting says U.S. equities were broadly flat to softer on July 23 ahead of major technology earnings, while earlier sessions saw global stocks retreat as investors reassessed geopolitical risk and inflation implications. Reuters also noted that the nearly five-month war has depleted global stockpiles and stoked inflation worldwide, linking the military escalation directly to macro pricing pressure rather than treating it as a contained oil-sector event. ([au.marketscreener.com](https://au.marketscreener.com/news/oil-prices-jump-on-us-iran-strikes-stocks-flat-ahead-of-big-tech-results-ce7f51d9dc8ff72c?utm_source=openai))

Other asset reactions are consistent with a classic conflict-inflation mix. Reuters reporting earlier in the renewed escalation cycle noted pressure on bonds and episodes of support for the dollar, while gold’s reaction has been complicated by higher oil feeding expectations of tighter-for-longer monetary policy. In practical terms, the dominant market signal today is that investors are pricing a prolonged disruption environment rather than an imminent negotiated settlement. No confirmed last-24-hour Reuters figure for WTI settlement was available in accessible sources, so Brent remains the clearest benchmark for the day’s move. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/stocks-bonds-retreat-after-trump-says-iran-mou-is-over-4781953?utm_source=openai))

## Consumer & Supply Chain Effects

The most important supply-chain fact remains that the Strait of Hormuz has been fully or partially closed for much of the conflict period, and the latest fighting is preventing normalization. AP reports that Southeast Asia is acutely exposed: the International Energy Agency estimates Asian markets imported roughly 80% of the crude oil and almost 90% of the LNG transiting Hormuz in 2025. That exposure explains why even incremental military escalation is still producing outsized downstream effects in Asia-Pacific fuel markets. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/12b3a257be0b6af9d96356dd78be3cfd?utm_source=openai))

In the last 24 hours, there were no widely confirmed new reports of mass fuel hoarding lines on the scale seen earlier in the war. However, AP reporting from the Manila diplomatic meetings said Southeast Asia continues to face a severe energy shock, and recalled that the Philippines declared a national energy emergency in March to prevent hoarding and profiteering. AP also reported this week that U.S. gasoline is back to an average of $4 a gallon, while shortages of essentials such as fertilizer have worsened. That points to sustained consumer stress even where panic buying is not newly visible today. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/788ceac7b1a80b74881bd5c69e334558?utm_source=openai))

Shipping disruption remains the central supply-chain mechanism. Recent tanker attacks in or near Hormuz, warnings affecting adjacent Red Sea traffic, and the Houthi threat to Bab el-Mandeb routes all indicate that rerouting risk now extends beyond a single chokepoint. U.S. blockade enforcement and Iranian route-control threats are compounding insurance, transit-time, and freight-cost pressures. For tomorrow, the key indicator will be whether any maritime authority or large carrier reports additional suspensions or revised routing guidance. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

## Diplomatic Developments

Diplomacy remains active but is not yet shaping battlefield behavior. The clearest reporting in the last 24-48 hours points to continuing mediation by Pakistan, Qatar, Egypt, and Oman, with AP describing efforts to salvage a collapsed interim ceasefire and Axios reporting that regional mediators have floated a 10-day ceasefire proposal. AP also reported that Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni visited Pakistan as Tehran sought to revive diplomacy, though there is no evidence in the last 24 hours of a breakthrough. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

At the UN level, the institution’s line remains de-escalatory. Earlier UN statements called for maximum restraint, protection of civilians, and implementation of existing ceasefire-related understandings. More recent UN coverage has kept the Hormuz crisis central, including discussion of broader regional energy-security consequences. However, there was no confirmed new Security Council action in the last 24 hours that materially altered the diplomatic landscape. ([dppa.un.org](https://dppa.un.org/en/speeches-and-statements/un-calls-for-maximum-restraint-to-preserve-ceasefire-between-the?utm_source=openai))

Regional Gulf states appear increasingly pessimistic. AP cited an Arab diplomat saying Gulf governments are worried that the latest threats leave little room for an off-ramp, especially as Iran has struck desalination and energy infrastructure in neighboring states. Meanwhile, U.S.-Pakistan coordination has broadened to include concern over Houthi pressure on Red Sea shipping, suggesting that mediators are now trying to contain a widening regional spillover rather than just negotiate a bilateral U.S.-Iran pause. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/42ff3de8d135ad72ff3ba4d94cc0921d?utm_source=openai))

## Humanitarian Situation

The humanitarian picture continues to worsen, but the last 24 hours produced little independently verified new casualty accounting. Where confirmed figures are unavailable, the appropriate assessment is: no confirmed reports in the last 24 hours of a new authoritative civilian casualty total. That said, the broader humanitarian baseline is severe. UNHCR said in March that up to 3.2 million Iranians had been temporarily displaced as the conflict intensified, and subsequent UNHCR situation reporting documented cross-border flows including tens of thousands of crossings involving Armenia by early July. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/news/press-releases/unhcr-3-2-million-iranians-temporarily-displaced-iran-conflict-intensifies?utm_source=openai))

Operational reporting indicates that both sides are increasingly threatening or striking infrastructure essential to civilian life. AP has reported attacks affecting power, transport, water, and desalination-linked systems, while the ICRC has repeatedly warned that renewed war would be ruinous for civilians and that hostilities are eroding the foundations of civilian life. These effects are often slower-moving than headline casualty counts but can prove more strategically destabilizing over time by driving displacement, disease risk, and economic collapse. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

Aid access remains constrained by insecurity and by the information blackout that has complicated verification inside Iran. UN reporting has continued to stress civilian protection and the need to respect international humanitarian law, but there was no confirmed last-24-hour announcement from UNHCR or the ICRC of a major new aid corridor, funding package, or evacuation arrangement. The humanitarian trendline is therefore negative even in the absence of fresh daily numbers: more displacement, more infrastructure degradation, and a shrinking margin of resilience for civilians inside Iran and in exposed neighboring states. ([un.org](https://www.un.org/en/security-council-holds-closed-door-talks-following-attacks-united-arab-emirates?utm_source=openai))

Outlook: Watch three indicators over the next 24 hours: whether CENTCOM escalates from infrastructure-degradation strikes to deeper leadership or nuclear-adjacent targets, whether Iran answers with a more direct missile or maritime action, and whether mediators can convert the reported 10-day truce concept into an actual pause. Markets will remain highly sensitive to any confirmed disruption in Hormuz tanker traffic, which is still the single fastest channel through which battlefield events are being transmitted into the global economy. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/42ff3de8d135ad72ff3ba4d94cc0921d?utm_source=openai))

briefingArchive.title: Day 144 Intelligence Briefing — July 22, 2026
briefingArchive.content:
The past 24 hours were defined by two reinforcing trends: a continued U.S. air campaign against Iranian military infrastructure around the Strait of Hormuz, and a renewed diplomatic push for a short ceasefire as the fighting’s economic and humanitarian costs climb. Markets are increasingly pricing the conflict not as a brief disruption but as a persistent threat to Gulf shipping, with Brent briefly approaching $92 a barrel while attacks on tankers and allied infrastructure continue. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

## Military Operations Summary

In the last 24 hours, the clearest confirmed military development was the continuation of U.S. strikes into an 11th consecutive night, with Washington framing the campaign as focused on degrading Iran’s ability to threaten shipping and regional bases. AP, citing U.S. officials, reported that the latest strike packages followed earlier waves targeting military command centers, missile and drone launch sites, maritime capabilities, and air-defense systems. Reuters reporting from July 20 described the previous round as hitting command centers, launch sites, maritime assets, and air defenses, suggesting the operational pattern remains centered on suppression of coastal and anti-access capabilities rather than deep strategic targets alone. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

The maritime picture also worsened. A tanker was attacked off Oman in or near the Strait of Hormuz, and the crew reportedly abandoned ship, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations channel as cited by AP. This indicates that despite repeated U.S. strikes, Iran or Iran-linked actors retain the capacity to menace commercial traffic in the strait. AP also reported Houthi threats to expand disruption to the Bab el-Mandeb, raising the possibility of simultaneous pressure on both ends of the Arabian Peninsula’s key maritime routes. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

There were no newly confirmed official disclosures in the last 24 hours on specific munitions used in the latest strikes. However, CENTCOM’s earlier public descriptions of this phase of the war indicate the campaign has included attacks on coastal radar, anti-ship missile systems, command-and-control nodes, and small-boat capabilities. That makes the current effort look like a sustained maritime-access air operation whose immediate objective is to reopen or secure shipping lanes rather than force regime collapse. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/commodities-news/us-says-it-has-completed-anew-round-of-strikes-on-iran-4780643?utm_source=openai))

## What Each Side Is Reporting

The U.S. and coalition narrative remains consistent: officials say the strikes are precision attacks intended to degrade Iran’s capacity to attack international shipping, U.S. positions, and allied interests. Pentagon messaging, reinforced during Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s Senate testimony on July 21, emphasizes that the campaign is necessary to protect navigation and respond to Iranian attacks that have now killed 17 U.S. service members, with AP also reporting the wounded total has climbed above 500 according to a U.S. official. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/7d158708c3e5385683930f8b839d0344?utm_source=openai))

Iranian messaging is more expansive and more overtly strategic. AP quoted a statement from Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warning that if the U.S. expands the war, all U.S., allied, and supporter interests in the region would become targets. Iranian state-linked narratives in recent reporting have stressed sovereign control over the Strait of Hormuz and portrayed U.S. operations as aggression rather than maritime security enforcement. Reuters reporting from recent days also captured Iranian threats to move into “full-scale offensive operations” if U.S. strikes continue. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/1664f6a4dad005a99771b2ad15213585?utm_source=openai))

Israeli official reporting in the last 24 hours was limited in publicly accessible primary-source material. No new IDF operational bulletin specific to July 21-22 was readily confirmed in the search results. The broader Israeli line remains that sustained air operations have significantly degraded Iranian missile and air-defense capacity, but for this briefing there are no confirmed fresh Israeli claims from the last 24 hours to detail.
